questions.q: What are the four parts of a DataFrame?
options: Rows, columns, index, and values
Rows, columns, keys, and functions
Series, lists, dictionaries, and tuples
Headers, footers, index, and formulas
questions.explain: Every DataFrame consists of rows (records), columns (named fields), the index (row labels), and the values sitting at each row/column intersection.

questions.q: What happens when you pull a single column out of a DataFrame?
options: It becomes a Series — Pandas' name for one column of labeled data on its own
It stays a DataFrame with just one column
It automatically converts to a Python list
Pandas throws an error, since columns can't be extracted individually
questions.explain: df["Revenue"] returns a Series, a distinct Pandas structure representing one labeled column — confirmed by checking its type().

questions.q: Is the DataFrame's index counted as one of its columns?
options: No — the index is row labels, separate from the columns, and by default is just row position, not meaningful data
Yes, the index always counts as the first column
Only if the DataFrame has fewer than 10 rows
The index and columns are the exact same thing
questions.explain: The index sits to the left of the actual columns and isn't included in a column count — it's a common point of confusion this lesson calls out directly.

options: A tuple of (row count, column count)
The names of every column
The data type of every column
The total sum of all numeric values
questions.explain: shape returns a tuple like (3, 3), meaning 3 rows and 3 columns — a quick way to size up a DataFrame without printing every row.

questions.q: What does df.dtypes show, and why does it matter for later lessons?
options: Each column's data type — Lesson 13 is built entirely around fixing columns whose type isn't what was expected
The number of duplicate rows in the DataFrame
Which columns contain missing values
The total file size of the DataFrame in memory
questions.explain: dtypes lists the data type of every column (object, int64, float64, etc.) — a critical check before cleaning data, since Lesson 13 focuses specifically on fixing mismatched types.
